title: Assessing Formal Thought Disorder in Clinical High-Risk Adolescents and Young Adults: A Scale-Guided Large Language Model Approach to Psychosis Prediction
content:
Background/Objectives: Formal thought disorder (FTD) is a clinically important feature of psychosis, but its assessment is time-intensive and dependent on trained raters. We hypothesized that a Thought and Language Disorder (TALD)-guided large language model (LLM) framework could identify clinically meaningful FTD features and distinguish healthy controls, clinical high-risk (CHR) non-converters, and CHR converters. Methods: The Story Game transcripts from 74 adolescents and young adults were analyzed, including 15 healthy controls (HC), 40 CHR non-converters (CHR−), and 19 CHR converters (CHR+). A modified 16-domain TALD framework was operationalized using a two-stage LLM agent that screened utterances and assigned domain-specific severity scores. Group differences were examined using sex-adjusted regression models with false discovery rate correction. Ten classifiers and seven feature sets were evaluated using repeated stratified five-fold cross-validation and leave-one-out cross-validation. 
Results: Significant sex-adjusted group effects were observed for Dissociation of Thinking, Poverty of Thought, and Verbigeration, which also ranked highest in the consensus feature-importance analysis. Classification performance was strongest for HC versus CHR (balanced accuracy = 0.881), followed by three-class classification of HC, CHR−, and CHR+ (0.753), and CHR− versus CHR+ classification (0.743). The three-class model exceeded chance performance in permutation testing (p = 0.005).
Conclusions: A TALD-guided LLM framework identified a focused set of clinically interpretable FTD features associated with psychosis-risk status and transition. These findings support the feasibility of scale-guided, transcript-based FTD assessment while underscoring the need for validation in larger and more diverse samples.
